chapter_theme: Paripadal 19, to Sevvel at Parankunram: the hill as heaven's gift to earth and its rival weddings, the pilgrims' road from Koodal, the Pandya king circling the hill, the painted hall with its explainers, the lost girl and the echo, the flowering slopes, the maidens' rite of the elephant's leftover, and the closing praise of the red god.

paripadal:19:1-18.reading: The poet says that at cool Parankunram, which the god seated by the famed kadambu gave so that the people of the wide earth too might share what the worthy of the sages' line enjoy, the adorned wedding with the peacock-like bride beside him seems to vie with that of the bride from heaven; and that at the end of night the crowds of Koodal, never beaten in learning or in war, go out in fine ornaments and bright cloth, on horses and in chariots, wearing chosen garlands and driving the dark from the streets, like doers of great aram setting out for the world of the excellent to take its fruit, so that the whole way from the hill to Koodal, packed with garlanded heads, is like a garland laid on the earth: the cool-sanded road the pilgrims take.
paripadal:19:1-18.nuance: The hill is framed as a gift: heaven's enjoyment brought within reach of ordinary people (lines 1 to 5). The peacock-creeper bride (மயிற்கொடி) is most likely Valli and the one of heaven (துறக்கத்தவள்) the daughter of Indra, so the earthly wedding is said to rival the heavenly one; the construal of lines 5 to 7 is not secure. The festival crowd is pictured through the reward of aram, riders in finery going to heaven, which turns a pilgrimage into a foretaste of the world to come.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's hill and of the pilgrimage to it, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the bride of the earthly wedding
the festival crowds setting out from Koodal
the unbroken line of garlanded heads on the road from the hill to Koodal

paripadal:19:19-37.reading: Like the stars that circle Meru with the sun, the Pandya Vazhuthi of the excellent land, with the women of his household gentle as young peahens and his officers who know their duty, climbs the broad slope of the god's hill where the fearful powers dwell and goes round it to the right, and the whole land and city arrive with cloths swaying on shoulders, singing tongues and spreading joy; and when one tells of the guarded town around the tall lord of the belled elephant, the ground below the hill, where people tie elephants to trees with flowered ropes, lead garlanded horses off the road, halt strong chariots along the way and feed mouthfuls of sugarcane, is like the camp of a king whose army has rearing horses: that is how we praise it.
paripadal:19:19-37.nuance: The king does not go before the god as a ruler receiving homage: he joins the circling crowd, and the poet likens his round to the stars that go round Meru with the sun, so the shrine becomes the centre and the Pandya one of its orbiting lights. The pilgrims' camp below the hill is in turn likened to a war camp, the king's world borrowed to describe a festival.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's procession round the god's hill, told as praise of the god

comparisons.tenor: the king and his train going round the hill
the women of the king's household
the crowded ground below the hill

paripadal:19:38-57.reading: Beside the temple of Maal Murugan on clear Parankunram stands a hall of paintings in its beauty: around it some give food to the monkeys and sugarcane to the black-faced langurs, some play the divine pirama, some set fingers to the flute, some tune the ili and kural strings of the lute, some speak of the beauty of the sacrifice, some beat the drum in order while the taut string hums, and some lose themselves in the picture of the wheel of the two lights that summer brings; some answer the curious who ask who is who, saying 'this is Rati and this Kama', and some explain 'this is Indra as a cat, she is Ahalya, he is Gautama who had gone out, and this is how she took the form of stone in his anger': many such paintings, drawn across the wide rooms of the facing rock, so that visitors point and are taught by pointing.
paripadal:19:38-57.nuance: This is one of the earliest Tamil records of a painted shrine hall and of how it was used: not only looked at but explained aloud, story by story, to visitors who asked (வினவ, வினா இறுப்போரும்; சுட்டவும், சுட்டு அறிவுறுத்தவும்). The paintings are of northern stories (Rati and Kama, Indra, Ahalya and Gautama) beside a Tamil god's temple. தெய்வப் பிரமம் (line 40) is read as a stringed instrument, and what the sun-and-moon picture shows (lines 46, 47) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's temple and its painted hall described as praise

paripadal:19:58-66.reading: A simple girl strays from the kin she came with, wanders in among the rocks and, lost, cries that she has forgotten even the path she came by, calling 'ee! oo!' to her people; the call that they do not take up is taken up by the echoing cave, which calls back, and she goes where it called, finds no kin there, turns back and calls 'koo, koo' once more: such, full of innocence, is the hill of the god who delights in praise.
paripadal:19:58-66.nuance: The innocence (மடமைத்தே) is given to the hill itself: the cave answers a call it does not understand, as artless as the girl who follows its answer, so the joke falls on the hill as much as on her. ஏலா அவ் விளி (line 62) is the call her kin do not answer.

thinai_evidence.note: a scene on the god's hill told as part of his praise

paripadal:19:67-84.reading: On the god's hill a branch bent at its tip with fragrant clusters sheds its shoots into a sweet pool, and the buds lifting their heads from the pool where they fell open as they lie, so that the young girls there are thrown into confusion and say 'chosen flowers and buds; no, a five-headed serpent with shining spots, the elder son, and beside it a young hatchling'; nearby, young pasumpidi buds, loose-mouthed water lilies, kaanthal clusters flowering like hands, fragrant eruvai blades, flame-clustered vengai, splendid thondri, narava in clusters, kongu that flowers out of season and the ilavam with its hostile red fill the slopes, crossing, rising and running on like flowers bound, strung, woven, hung and mixed, and the hill shines like the wide sky at dawn.
paripadal:19:67-84.nuance: The girls' mistake is turned into a small family: a five-headed snake, its elder son and a young hatchling, read off a cluster of floating buds. The list of flowers is the hill's own garland, made by no hand yet described in the five ways garland makers work them.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering of the god's hill described as praise

comparisons.tenor: the floating buds in the pool

paripadal:19:85-105.reading: When a man of full heart comes to make a rite, painting the head of your elephant with kunkumam, giving it flower-water, setting chowries on it and raising a golden umbrella on a staff of gold and coral, the maidens with long dark tresses of many scents, whose maidenhood has ripened, will not reach the arms of spotless young men, and the wives will not win the smiling grace of those who married them, unless they come near your hill and eat as a sacred thing the leftover of the mouthful taken by the elephant that bears your banner; you who joined the creeper of a kurava girl, take in with your ear the praise as your sacred food: your dress and cloak are red, your weapon takes the colour of the coral creeper, your form is like fire and your face like the spreading sun before its rays are full; you who cut down the great mango-root of the matchless foe, drove your spear into the hostile hill and broke it, we have told your beautiful stance by the kadambu on this hill and have praised you, worshipping, together with our company.
paripadal:19:85-105.nuance: Two kinds of sacred food are set side by side: the girls must eat the elephant's leftover as சிறப்பு உணா to win husbands, and the god is asked to take the singers' praise as his சிறப்பு உணா through the ear (lines 94 to 96). வாரணம் (line 91) could also mean the cock of his banner, but கவழம், a mouthful, fits the elephant whose decoration opens the passage. The red god of lines 97 to 100 is the image at the shrine, addressed by a company of worshippers.

thinai_evidence.note: closing praise and worship of the god, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the praise offered to the god
the colour of the god's weapon

links.note: Paripadal 9.8-11 says that when the god married the fawn-like girl, the eyes of the daughter of the thousand-eyed one rained like rain in summer at Parankunram; Paripadal 19.5-7 says the wedding with the peacock-like bride at the same hill seems to vie with that of the bride from heaven.
links.teaches: In song 9 the second marriage is a wound to the first wife, while song 19 turns the same two weddings into a contest of splendour in which the earthly bride matches the heavenly one, so the hill's lore of two marriages could be sung either as a domestic grief or as the claim that Parankunram brings heaven's festival down to earth.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 71-77 places the god's hill west of Koodal of crowded mansion streets, among wide muddy fields of lotus and bees; Paripadal 19.8-18 fills the whole stretch between the hill and Koodal (குன்றொடு கூடல் இடையெல்லாம்) with a pre-dawn procession of riders, chariots and garlanded heads.
links.teaches: The guide poem gives the pilgrim the hill's place relative to the city and its quiet fields, and the hymn shows the same stretch on festival day as one continuous human garland, so together they show Parankunram as Madurai's own shrine, whose road from the city was itself part of the festival.

links.note: Kural 37 tells us to see the way of aram in the difference between the one who bears the palanquin and the one who rides in it; Paripadal 19.10-13 likens the festival riders on horses and in chariots, in fine ornament and cloth, to those who have done much aram and set out for the world of the excellent to take its fruit.
links.teaches: Both picture the fruit of aram as riding in finery, but the Paripadal puts that ride in the passage to the next world and uses it only as a simile for festival-goers, while the Kural reads it in this world's ranks, so the pair shows the Kural's hard claim taking a shared image of heavenly reward and pressing it into a judgement on living people.

links.note: Kural 25 names Indra, lord of the wide heaven, as witness enough to the strength of one who has quenched the five senses; Paripadal 19.50-52 records visitors at the Parankunram painted hall explaining a picture: Indra as the cat, Ahalya, Gautama who had gone out, and her form turned to stone in his anger.
links.teaches: On the reading that Indra is witness through his own fall, the Kural's single name assumes a story that the Paripadal shows painted on a Madurai temple wall and told aloud to anyone who asked, so the couplet's allusion was not learned lore but a tale ordinary pilgrims were taught from pictures.

links.note: Paripadal 8.19-21 has the hill's caves (மலை முழை) answer back and forth the cock's crow and the musth elephants' trumpeting that answer the god's elephant and the thunder; Paripadal 19.62-65 has the echoing cave (இசை முழை) take up a lost girl's call and lead her astray.
links.teaches: In song 8 the cave echo multiplies the god's elephant, his cock and the storm into a sign that the whole hill answers him, while in song 19 the same caves fool a lost girl and the poet calls this the hill's innocent nature, so the pair shows the Parankunram echo used both as a mark of divine presence and as the hill's playful character.

links.note: In Akananuru 98 the girl fears that if Murugan, the tall Vel smelling of veri, should actually relieve her at the mother's rite, her lover will hear that her pain was something else; Paripadal 19.89-94 says maidens will not reach young men's arms, nor wives their husbands' grace, unless they eat the leftover of the god's elephant at his hill.
links.teaches: The akam girl's dread makes sense only if Murugan really does rule a girl's union, and the Paripadal states that power openly as a festival rite that maidens and wives perform, so together they show that the akam irony about the veri rite rests on a public belief in the god as the giver of husbands, not on disbelief in him.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 206-217 describes the god as red, in red clothing (செய்யன் சிவந்த ஆடையன்), dancing on every hill with the women's soft shoulders in his arms; Paripadal 19.97-100 tells him his dress and cloak are red, his weapon coral-coloured, his form like fire and his face like the young sun.
links.teaches: The guide poem's red god is roaming from hill to hill in the kurinji dance, while the hymn addresses the same red figure as the image standing by the kadambu at one shrine, praised by a gathered company, so the pair shows one colour iconography carried from the wandering god of the hill people to the fixed god of a temple.

source_issues: Paripadal 19: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; only the subject செவ்வேள், the poet நப்பண்ணனார், the music by மருத்துவன் நல்லச்சுதனார் and the pan காந்தாரம் (a musical mode, not a thinai).
Paripadal 19 lines 9, 39 and 68 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags). Lines 8, 20, 32, 41 and 89 are flagged as near a dropped modern heading; check by eye.
Paripadal 19 line 6: -ளொடு restored by rule in துறக்கத்தவளொடு, not confirmed by sangamtamil.com (flag).
Paripadal 19 line 43: வேள்லியின் reads as a misprint for வேள்வியின்.
Paripadal 19 line 85: நின யானைச் reads as a misprint for நின் யானைச்; குங்குமத் தால் is split for குங்குமத்தால்.

Paripadal 19 lines 24-25 (பழ மதிச் சூடி அசையும் சுவல்மிசைத் தானையின்), 30 (தும்பி twice, bee or elephant), 40 (தெய்வப் பிரமம்) and 67-73 (பல்லவன் and the girls' words) are hard to construe; the readings given are provisional.
